findings.title: Database writes and ZADD queue:priority:<tier> can get out of step
findings.consequence: `INSERT jobs`, `UPDATE jobs SET status='pending', attempts by id + status` and `UPDATE jobs SET status='pending', error by id` each commit first, then Redis is updated in a separate call. If Redis is down or the process dies in between, the two disagree: the row says one thing, Redis another, and nothing repairs it later. The caller may also get an error for work that was in fact saved.
findings.fix: Make the database the source of truth and rebuild Redis from it: write an outbox row in the same transaction and let a worker update Redis, or run a periodic job that re-syncs Redis from the database.

findings.title: Every open tab polls GET /stats every 5 s on top of its live WebSocket
findings.consequence: The browser asks whether anything changed even when nothing did. 10,000 open tabs make about 2,000 requests per second to GET /stats, most returning the same data. Cost grows with users, not with how often data changes. This page already receives pushed updates, so the timer mostly repeats work.
findings.fix: Send what GET /stats returns over the socket (or push a snapshot every few seconds from the server). If the timer also catches things the socket can't report, keep it but slow it down.

findings.title: Each pushed message makes every browser call GET /stats
findings.consequence: The server pushes an event and every connected page answers by requesting GET /stats. 100 open dashboards and 20 events per second become 2,000 requests per second to GET /stats, more load than polling would cause.
findings.fix: Send the data the page needs inside the pushed message, refresh only for the message types that change it, or debounce the refresh.

findings.title: idx_jobs_status duplicates idx_jobs_status_priority_run_at on jobs
findings.consequence: idx_jobs_status_priority_run_at starts with the same columns, so one of the two never helps a read. Every insert and update still maintains both, which costs write time and disk. No query here filters or sorts on priority and run_at, so the longer index is the one doing no work.

findings.title: SELECT jobs by status, page (LIMIT/OFFSET) sorts without a matching index
findings.consequence: No index hands rows out in id order within status, so to return the first page the database may have to collect every matching row of jobs and sort them before the LIMIT applies. Then each page costs as much as reading all of them.
findings.fix: Add an index on the filter columns followed by the sort columns, in a new migration: CREATE INDEX ON jobs (status, id);

findings.title: Worker checks Redis for work every 1 s even when there is none
findings.consequence: An idle worker keeps asking Redis whether there's work, and a new job waits up to 1 s before a worker notices it. Each extra idle worker adds the same steady trickle of empty reads.
findings.fix: Wake idle workers when work arrives (a pub/sub message, LISTEN/NOTIFY, or a blocking pop where the data structure allows it) and keep a slower timer as a fallback for delayed jobs.

flows.summary: The worker handles one job at a time: poll() awaits runOnce() and then re-arms itself with setTimeout, 0 ms if it processed a job and 1000 ms if the queue was empty. runOnce asks Redis for the earliest due id in priority tiers 0-9, flips that Postgres row from 'pending' to 'processing' (attempts + 1) with a guarded UPDATE, and ZREMs the id whether or not the UPDATE matched, looping past stale ids. The handler is picked by job.type; success sets status 'completed' and clears error, while a throw either dead-letters the job ('failed') once attempts >= max_attempts or sets it back to 'pending' with run_at pushed out by exponential backoff and re-adds it to Redis. Every transition publishes on 'job:events', and a scheduled retry is published as 'job:failed' even though the row is 'pending' again.

flows.summary: On load the page fetches GET /jobs?limit=20 (newest 20 rows, ORDER BY id DESC) and GET /stats in parallel and renders the job table, per-status counts and worker list. loadInitial is not awaited, so the page opens a WebSocket to ws://<same host> at the same time: a live event that arrives before the GET /jobs answer is overwritten by that older snapshot. On the server side the server only adds the socket to an in-memory Set and removes it on close. After this first fetch the job table is only patched from WebSocket events, and the 2 s auto-reconnect does not call loadInitial again, so job changes missed while disconnected stay stale until a full page reload. The ws:// scheme is hard-coded, so the live connection would be blocked if the page were served over HTTPS.

flows.summary: The API process subscribes to Redis channel 'job:events' on its own duplicated connection, because a subscribed Redis connection cannot run normal commands. Each message is JSON-parsed; 'worker:heartbeat' messages also update the in-memory last-seen map, and every message (heartbeats included) is sent to every open WebSocket. In the browser, job:* events patch only id, type, status and updated_at of that row (so attempts and priority go stale, or show '-' for jobs created after load), and every message triggers GET /stats to refresh counts and workers. Redis Pub/Sub keeps no history, so events published while the API is down or while a browser is reconnecting are simply lost.

flows.summary: This is the manual dead-letter recovery path: one UPDATE resets status to 'pending', attempts to 0, clears error and sets run_at = now(), but only WHERE status = 'failed'. If no row matches (unknown id, or a job that is pending, processing or completed) it returns 404 'no dead-lettered job with this id'; otherwise it ZADDs the job back into its Redis tier, publishes the event as 'job:created' (there is no separate retried event) and returns 200 with the row. Because of the status guard, jobs stuck in 'processing' cannot be recovered through this endpoint.

flows.summary: Runs SELECT status, count(*) FROM jobs GROUP BY status and returns 200 with {counts, workers}; statuses that have no jobs are simply absent from counts (the dashboard fills them with 0). workers comes from the API process's in-memory heartbeat map, and a worker is reported online if its last heartbeat was within 15 s, computed at request time. That map is never pruned and every worker start gets a fresh random UUID, so restarted workers pile up as 'offline' entries until the API itself restarts.

flows.summary: Each open dashboard runs setInterval(refreshStats, 5000), which fetches GET /stats and re-renders the queue-depth counts and worker list; it never touches the job table. Because online/offline is computed only when /stats is called, this poll is what eventually flips a worker to 'offline' in the UI when heartbeats stop and no other events arrive (after the 15 s window). refreshStats has no .catch: if the request fails on the network the last values stay on screen, but if /stats answers 500 the counts panel is cleared and the worker list goes stale.

flows.summary: Serves the single static file api/public/dashboard.html with res.sendFile; there is no static-asset directory, build step or authentication. All CSS and JavaScript are inline in that file, and once loaded it starts the page-load flow (GET /jobs, GET /stats, WebSocket) and the 5 s stats poll. express.json runs first for every route but does nothing for a GET without a JSON body.

Every 5 s each worker publishes {type: 'worker:heartbeat', workerId, at} on 'job:events', where workerId is a random UUID generated at process start. The API records the time in its in-memory map (a worker counts as online for 15 s after a heartbeat) and also forwards the heartbeat to every connected browser. Because it is a separate setInterval it keeps firing while a job is being processed; publish errors are only logged, and the interval is cleared when shutdown begins.

insights.title: Jobs can be stuck in 'processing' forever
insights.explanation: Claiming sets the row to 'processing' and removes the id from Redis before the handler runs; no code ever looks for or resets 'processing' rows, and the manual retry only matches status = 'failed'. A worker killed by SIGKILL/OOM/crash mid-job (only SIGTERM and SIGINT are handled), or a recordFailure call that throws (the error escapes runOnce and poll only logs it), leaves the job stranded. There is also no handler timeout, so a hung handler blocks that worker permanently and graceful shutdown waits on it forever.

insights.title: Claim race: peek is not a pop, and the guard ignores run_at
insights.explanation: peekDueJob only reads the head of a tier (ZRANGEBYSCORE LIMIT 1) without removing it, so every idle worker gets the same id and they race on the same row; losers spend an UPDATE and a ZREM and loop. The claim UPDATE checks status = 'pending' but not run_at, and ZREM deletes the id whatever its score. So a worker with a stale peek, if another worker has meanwhile claimed, failed and re-queued that job with backoff, can claim it immediately (skipping the backoff), or, if its UPDATE missed but its ZREM lands after the re-ZADD, delete the new retry entry and leave a 'pending' row no worker will ever see.

insights.title: Unknown job types are accepted, retried, or silently 'completed'
insights.explanation: POST /jobs only checks that type is a non-empty string, so a typo like 'send_mail' gets 201 and then fails every attempt with 'no handler registered' until it is dead-lettered. Deterministic payload errors such as a missing payload.to take the same retry-with-backoff path and burn all attempts. Because handlers is a plain object indexed with handlers[job.type], the types 'toString' or 'constructor' resolve to inherited Object.prototype functions and the job is marked 'completed' without any real handler running.

insights.title: Priority is clamped to 10 tiers and strictly ordered
insights.explanation: Any integer priority is accepted and stored as-is, but Redis clamps it into tiers 0-9, so priority -50 behaves like 0 and 1000 like 9 while the API and dashboard show the raw number. Lower numbers are more urgent: claimNextJob scans tier 0 first and returns the first due job, so a steady stream of due tier-0 jobs starves the other tiers indefinitely (there is no aging). Inside a tier, order is by run_at only.

insights.title: Retry timing: uncapped, unjittered backoff judged on two clocks
insights.explanation: The delay is 5 * 2^(attempts-1) seconds with no cap or jitter, and maxAttempts has no upper bound; with the default max_attempts of 3 a job retries after 5 s and 10 s, but one allowed 20 attempts waits 5 * 2^18 s (about 15 days) after its 19th failure. Jobs that fail together, e.g. during a downstream outage, all retry at the same instant. run_at is computed with Postgres now() and used as the Redis score, but due-ness is judged against the worker's Date.now(), so clock skew between the DB host and worker hosts makes jobs run early or late.
